neurological_exam.additional: Found unresponsive at home. Serum sodium 110 mEq/L on admission — profound hyponatremia. SIADH confirmed. Hydrochlorothiazide was held on admission but sodium had been stable for 3 months prior on the same regimen. patient.chief_complaint: Found unresponsive at home with serum sodium 110 mEq/L (profound hyponatremia), confusion, and on day 6 developed bilateral lower limb weakness and areflexia.
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. R. is a 64-year-old woman found unresponsive at home by her neighbor. She reported mild malaise, decreased appetite, and mild stomach discomfort the day prior. On emergency evaluation, she was obtunded (GCS 9) with confused speech. Laboratory studies revealed profound hyponatremia with serum sodium 110 mEq/L — markedly below her last documented value of 136 mEq/L three months prior on the same medication regimen. Serum osmolality was 235 mOsm/kg. Urine osmolality 413 mOsm/kg with high urine sodium consistent with SIADH. CT head and neck were normal. MRI brain showed multiple nonspecific T2 hyperintensities without osmotic demyelination. EEG showed mild diffuse slowing — no epileptiform discharges. CSF on day 1 showed protein 52 mg/dL with 1 WBC. Initial management focused on SIADH treatment with hydrochlorothiazide discontinuation, hypertonic saline, and IV antibiotics (empiric). Sodium was corrected from 110 to 124 mEq/L over 24 hours — within safe range (10 mEq/L/24h). By hospital day 5 she was improving cognitively and transferred to the ward. However, on day 6 she complained of new lower back pain followed by bilateral leg numbness and tingling and gait instability. Neurological examination then revealed bilateral lower limb weakness and areflexia — findings not present at admission. The temporal dissociation between the presenting encephalopathy (from profound hyponatremia) and the delayed emergence of GBS motor/sensory findings creates a diagnostic puzzle: the GBS was clinically hidden behind the dominant presenting problem of hyponatremic encephalopathy.

critical_actions: Recognize that profound SIADH can be the PRESENTING feature of GBS before motor symptoms appear — GBS autonomic dysfunction dysregulates ADH
Day 1 CSF protein was elevated (52 mg/dL) before neurological motor symptoms developed — the diagnosis was available from the beginning
Safe sodium correction rate is critical: max 10 mEq/L per 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome
IVIG must not be delayed once GBS is confirmed — even if sodium is still being corrected
Monitor for osmotic demyelination (CPM/EPM) with MRI spine — symptoms emerging after correction may be GBS not CPM
contraindicated_actions: Rapid sodium correction (>10 mEq/L/24h) — risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome
key_reasoning_points: GBS autonomic dysfunction can cause SIADH — hypothalamic ADH regulation is disrupted by the autoimmune process affecting autonomic nerves
The profound hyponatremia (Na 110) dominated the presentation and masked the underlying GBS — neurological symptoms emerged only after sodium was corrected
Day 1 CSF had albumino-cytologic dissociation (protein 52, WBC 1) — GBS was already present but unrecognized because motor exam was limited by encephalopathy
Distinguish osmotic demyelination syndrome (rapid correction complication) from GBS-related weakness emerging after correction — MRI spine is key
Thiazide diuretics may worsen hyponatremia in patients with GBS-associated SIADH — hold HCTZ permanently in GBS
